# Summary: Labour Party Manifesto 2010 – "A Future Fair for All"

## Context and Vision

The 2010 Labour manifesto was published during a period of unprecedented challenges: British troops serving in Afghanistan, the aftermath of the global financial crisis, and a political system damaged by the expenses scandal. Labour positioned itself as the party of progressive change, rejecting "business as usual" and proposing transformative reforms across the economy, society, and politics. The core vision is a modern, progressive Britain built on fairness, respect, and active government intervention.

## Economic Recovery and Reform

Labour's central economic argument rejects immediate spending cuts, positioning the Conservatives as recklessly threatening recovery. Instead, Labour commits to halving the deficit over four years through growth, fair taxation (including the new 50p top tax rate), and targeted cuts to lower priorities—not frontline services.

Fundamental banking reform is proposed: stricter regulation, "living wills" for failing banks, a global financial levy, and breaking up government-controlled banks. Labour champions a new industrial strategy, including £4 billion for UK Finance for Growth to support businesses, expanded R&D tax credits, and investment in green industries, digital infrastructure, and high-speed rail. The goal is one million skilled jobs by 2015, with particular focus on low-carbon and high-tech sectors.

## Social Justice and Public Services

Labour pledges to protect frontline spending on the NHS, schools, policing, and childcare. Healthcare reforms include legally binding patient guarantees, expanded GP access, and personalised care. In education, every child is guaranteed catch-up tuition if falling behind, and failing schools will be taken over by proven providers.

On welfare, Labour proposes ending long-term unemployment through mandatory job placements and raising the minimum wage in line with earnings. A new National Care Service would provide free home care for those with greatest needs and cap residential care costs.

## Political Reform

Responding to the expenses crisis, Labour proposes referenda on electoral reform (Alternative Vote) and an elected House of Lords, fixed-term parliaments, a statutory lobbyist register, and exploration of a written constitution—aiming to restore trust and accountability in politics.
